This section collects key analytical questions in this 

shared google document, open for additions, relevant to the 2026 DRC Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak response.

The questions within 

the document were compiled with input from individuals with operational and analytical experience in country-level response. No formal consensus or agreement process was conducted beyond these individual consultations. As such, the questions are intended to help guide and coordinate analytical efforts while reflecting suggestions from the wider community.

Please review the questions and indicate where you are currently working or planning to work by adding your information in 

this link. This input will be compiled into an overview to help the community understand who is working on which topics and to identify potential gaps or bottlenecks. The objective is to support better coordination and enable more targeted collaboration where specific insights are needed for the response.

Please feel free to add lines in the 

google sheet if the line corresponding to the question you want to answer is already used.

By contributing your information, you agree to it being shared on Collaboratory. If you have any questions, please contact 

collaboratory@who​.int.

Welcome to the Ebola Outbreak Analytics Community Resources Collection. This is a curated, community-maintained collection of resources supporting analytics for the 2026 Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The purpose of these pages is to collate information relevant to outbreak analytics and make it more easily accessible in a single location.

We do not own, produce, or endorse the information presented here, all resources are publicly available and are simply aggregated and organized for the benefit of the response community.

This site is maintained by the Ebola Outbreak Analytics Community of Practice (CoP) within the 

Collaboratory.

While this collection is reviewed and updated regularly by community members, we cannot guarantee that all information is complete, accurate, or fully up to date at all times. If you notice missing resources, outdated information, or inaccuracies, we encourage you to contribute and help improve the collection.

We invite all colleagues currently involved in outbreak analytics, as well as those interested in sharing expertise from previous outbreak responses, to join our Community of Practice (CoP) on the WHO Collaboratory.

To become a member:

Register for the WHO Collaboratory by following the 

registration instructions.

Access the 

Collaboratory.

Join the 

Ebola Outbreak Analytics Community.

Share your work, attend community meetings, and learn what others are working on.

The easiest way to contribute is to 

open a GitHub Issue. Just fill in the form — no coding needed. A maintainer will review and add it to the site.

See 

Contributing for more details.

If you are familiar with GitHub and would like to contribute more actively, we also welcome support with reviewing, discussing, and helping to resolve issues. Your contributions can help improve the platform and strengthen the outbreak analytics community.

A community member opens a GitHub Issue using the “Suggest a Resource” form

A GitHub Action creates a .md file in the appropriate section directory, appends an {include} directive to the section’s index file, and opens a Pull Request

The maintainer reviews the PR — checks that the file is in the right section and the {include} is placed correctly — and merges

A deploy workflow builds and publishes the updated site

For resources submitted as “Other / New section”, the file goes to docs/_incoming/ and no index file is modified — the maintainer places it manually.
Technical contributors may open PRs with new .md files or edits to existing ones. The maintainer adds an {include} directive to the appropriate section index file during review.

myst.yml                    ← site config + TOC (references index files only)
assets/
  logo.png                  ← site logo and static assets
docs/
  intro.md                  ← landing page
  contributing.md
  maintainers.md
  analytical-questions.md
  _incoming/                ← staging area for automation-created files
  resources/                ← all contributed content
    tools-index.md          ← section index: Resources and tools
    data-index.md           ← section index: Data
    evidence-synthesis-index.md  ← section index: Evidence Synthesis
    community-meetings-index.md ← section index: Community meeting materials
    dashboards/             ← one .md file per resource
    epi-parameters/
    outbreak-size-estimates/
    risk-of-spread/
    mobility-data/
    humanitarian-data/
    therapeutics-vaccines/

Each section has an index file (e.g. tools-index.md) that uses {include} directives to pull in individual resource files. This means:

All resources in a section render as one continuous page in the sidebar

Individual resource files stay separate for easy editing and version control

The sidebar shows one entry per section, not one per resource

Outbreak Size: At a glance

Reported case counts still understate true infections, with the gap holding roughly steady. The under-ascertainment ratio stands at 1.6–3.3× against 8,978 confirmed cases as of 10 October, based on a 90% credible interval of 14,028–29,258 cumulative infections. Ten separate analyses suggest persistent under-detection, with moderate confidence that under-detection persists at a roughly stable level.

Read the full synthesis

Risk of Spread: At a glance

Nearby countries, particularly Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, face the highest near-term risk of imported Bundibugyo virus cases from the DRC. Rankings for more distant countries vary across analyses, driven by differences in how each model treats air travel, land travel, and the assumed spatial distribution of source cases. Evidence suggests that surveillance is best concentrated on the highest-probability importation routes. Confidence is moderate, with relative destination rankings holding up better across analyses than the absolute probabilities attached to them.

Read the full synthesis

Collaboratory.

Pages are updated within one working day of new or revised analyses appearing. Verify figures and interpretations against the referenced analyses before use in operational decisions.

These pages are produced by a semi-automated evidence-synthesis pipeline that pairs AI models with human review at each major checkpoint: one model reads each source analysis on its own and grounds every extracted claim in a verbatim quoted passage; a second model takes the resulting structured comparison as input, and drafts the narrative. Human analysts then review and edit the output to ensure accuracy and completeness prior to publishing.

Identifying analyses. Analyses are identified through continuous monitoring of preprint servers, peer-reviewed publications, and grey literature. An analysis is included if it directly addresses the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak and provides a quantitative estimate relevant to a given topic (e.g., outbreak size, risk of spread). Each included source is logged, and if the authors later release an updated version, the newer version supersedes the earlier one.

Preparing the source text. Each source text, regardless of source type (e.g., PDF, HTML), is converted to Markdown. A human analyst then curates the converted file and removes sections that carry no evidentiary content, such as references, acknowledgments, author contributions, affiliations, and declarations of interest, to keep extraction focused and reduce the number of input tokens used.

Extracting structured evidence. The curated text is split into individually citeable units, one per sentence, and passed to Claude Sonnet 4.6. For each of a fixed set of dimensions (e.g., estimates, methods, limitations), the model answers from that one source alone and must ground every factual claim in a verbatim span of its text.

Synthesizing the narrative. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 model reads the dimensions extracted for each analysis and synthesizes the information, covering the state of the evidence, how the estimates compare and why they diverge, the key uncertainties and assumptions shared across analyses, what would most reduce that uncertainty, and what it implies for the response.

Human review and publication. Human analysts edit the draft for accuracy, completeness, and tone prior to publishing.

Limitations. This pipeline surfaces only publicly available analyses; works that have not been made public are not captured.

The body of evidence comprises ten analyses, including peer-reviewed studies, preprints and two online dashboards, posted from 24 May to 10 October 2026. Only McCabe et al., Abbott et al., Epistorm, Oraby et al. and Kim et al. estimate true outbreak size or an upper bound of it. Mooring et al. and Chamla et al. project future trajectories, while the three Verheyden preprints address growth, fatality ratios or forecasting of confirmed counts to give wider context on the question of outbreak size.

Abbott et al. estimate roughly 1.6–3.3× as many infections as laboratory-confirmed cases at 10 October. McCabe et al. estimated about 280–2,520 cases at 27 May, against 1,031 suspected-or-confirmed reported cases, so the range spans values below and above the reported figure. Chamla et al. report that the suspected count peaked at 1,077 on 26 May and was then sharply revised downward, so the laboratory-confirmed series became the reliable comparator; a suspected-or-confirmed denominator such as McCabe et al.'s is therefore not equivalent to a confirmed count. Oraby et al. estimate 1,120 cumulative infections at the fitted rate at which patients leave isolation against 896 confirmed cases as of 17 June, without stating a ratio. The analyses differ in denominator, geography and method, and the denominator alone matters: Chamla et al.'s published quantity is the confirmed-case count, which excludes the unconfirmed and unascertained cases that Abbott et al. and McCabe et al. estimate.

Most of the uncertainty is structural rather than statistical, and four assumptions are shared widely enough that their failure would move several estimates together.

First, the analyses make different assumptions about detection, so their estimates are not measuring quite the same thing. Chamla et al. set the reporting fraction at 1.0, which limits their quantity to confirmed cases; Epistorm’s second calibration stage allows ascertainment as low as 40%; and Abbott et al. have no line list or reporting-completeness data to anchor detection, so their multiplier of roughly 1.6–3.3 infections per confirmed case is a model-based extrapolation.

Second, death-based estimates rest on borrowed parameters. McCabe et al. assume a case fatality ratio and onset-to-death delay consistent with earlier Bundibugyo outbreaks and an assumed epidemic doubling time of 7–14 days (a 10-day doubling time in the main scenario), and the estimated size rises with a lower ratio, faster growth, or a higher share of deaths due to Ebola. Abbott et al. likewise use weakly informed priors for delays and the ratio, often from other outbreaks, and their posteriors largely track those priors.

Third, travel-based inference assumes every resident is equally likely to travel regardless of infection status, which healthcare-seeking behaviour violates. Short trips also let infected travellers return home before detection, and accounting for trip durations raised Kim et al.'s central estimates and widened their confidence intervals.

Finally, model simplifications limit what the estimates can show. Chamla et al. assume homogeneous mixing and uniform response intensity, which oversimplify spatial heterogeneity across health zones, and anchoring on a single confirmed-case datum makes their fit sensitive to that anchor. Oraby et al. add that the undetected burden, postmortem detection and funeral infectiousness cannot be separately identified, so several parameters were fixed or strongly regularized.

Chamla et al. and Verheyden and Mudogo both name line-list data as a priority, with Chamla et al. adding contact-tracing data. Additionally, in line with their shared uncertainties, would be outbreak-specific cross-border movement data, because travel-based methods are limited by poorly understood crossing dynamics and the export stream in Abbott et al. rests on a traveller volume taken from McCabe et al.

The authors’ open questions converge on better linked data. McCabe et al. call for epidemic size, growth rate, and geography to be characterised with epidemiological and genomic data, while Chamla et al. call for line lists, contact-tracing data, and dynamic mobility estimates. Verheyden and Mudogo identify patient-linked records as necessary for causal attribution of fatality differences.

Abbott et al. (10 Oct 2026)Estimating the current size of the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo virus outbreak

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis estimates how many people have been infected in the DRC outbreak, reported and unreported, and how that compares with laboratory-confirmed cases. It fits a single statistical model of how infections spread to several streams of situation-report counts and to cases exported to Uganda. The outbreak is estimated to have caused 30% 18406-21567, 60% 16546-23965, 90% 14028-29258 infections to date, reported and unreported. Against the 8978 laboratory-confirmed cases by the cut-off, that is roughly 1.6-3.3× as many infections.

Headline (joint model, DRC nationally, data as of 10 October 2026): Cumulative infections, reported and unreported, are estimated at 30% 18406-21567, 60% 16546-23965, 90% 14028-29258. Against the 8978 laboratory-confirmed cases by the cut-off, this is roughly 1.6-3.3× as many infections, so confirmed cases are estimated to capture only a small share of the outbreak.

Other quantities reported at the same cut-off:

The outbreak is estimated to have begun between 2026-03-01 and 2026-03-27 (90% interval), an elapsed age of 197-223 days.

The initial reproduction number was 30% 1.91-2.18, 60% 1.79-2.38, 90% 1.59-2.73, and the latest is 30% 1.05-1.2, 60% 0.97-1.3, 90% 0.83-1.52.

The latest growth rate is 30% 0.003-0.014, 60% -0.002-0.021, 90% -0.013-0.035 per day.

The case-fatality ratio is 30% 0.46-0.51, 60% 0.43-0.54, 90% 0.39-0.6.

The page does not give numeric infection estimates for the earlier frozen cut-offs or the per-stream fits in the text provided.

Joint Bayesian multi-patch renewal model: This is a real-time, joint Bayesian model that began as a replication of McCabe and others (2026). One joint model is fitted to every national data stream and the provincial tables, on a daily grid from a seeding date to the cut-off. Each patch runs its own renewal equation, with a reproduction number that is a shared weekly trend times a deviation for that patch. Each data stream sees a delayed or thinned view of the same patch infections. The streams include suspected and confirmed cases and deaths, laboratory volumes, treatment-centre flows, a digitised symptom-onset curve and Uganda exports. Outbreak size and each system’s reporting fraction are estimated jointly. It covers the DRC nationally by province, with Uganda exports as an additional data stream. Importation couples the patches by moving a share of each day’s new infections from one patch to another. The outbreak is assumed to have started from a zoonotic spillover and to have grown through an unobserved cryptic exponential phase. A genetic bound bounds the cryptic phase from below.

Health-zone model: A second model splits the joint model’s infections in each patch across the health zones of that patch. It is fitted after the joint model, to the same cut-off, and does not feed back into it. It uses the cumulative confirmed cases and deaths for each health zone from the situation reports. It produces zone-level reproduction numbers and one-week forecasts.

Single-stream fits, frozen re-fits and forecasts: Single-stream models are written for each count-based stream, so each stream’s posterior outbreak size can be compared with the joint. Frozen re-fits cut the data to an earlier cut-off and re-fit the joint model. Forecasts are drawn from the fitted model itself.

Generation interval and seeding: The generation interval is a Gamma with a sampled mean and SD, taken from the Ebola virus disease serial interval used as a generation-time proxy (mean 15.3 d, SD 9.3 d). The outbreak is assumed to have started from a zoonotic spillover and grown deterministically through an unobserved cryptic exponential phase. The origin prior is centred so the implied origin sits in mid-February, with 90% of its mass between mid-January and mid-March. The initial growth rate has a log-normal prior equivalent to a doubling time centred on 11.7 d. The authors state the model inherits McCabe et al.'s assumptions of a single zoonotic seed and a generation interval from earlier Ebola outbreaks, which help constrain the estimated outbreak age and early reproduction number.

Genetic bound on outbreak age: The TMRCA is treated as a lower bound on the outbreak age, leaving the age free above it. The molecular clock is fixed to the rate of the 2013-2016 West African Ebola epidemic. The authors state they fix the clock and do not propagate cross-outbreak or clock uncertainty.

Response effect on transmission: The response is assumed to take about three weeks (21 days) to take effect and to be able only to reduce transmission. The ramp is fixed in time, with an assumed start and three-week duration, and only its size is estimated.

Incubation and other delays: Incubation uses the 2007 Uganda outbreak estimate (mean 6.3 d). Onset-to-admission is a Gamma centred on the Isiro reanalysis posterior (implied mean about 4 d). Onset-to-death is the convolution of onset-to-admission and admission-to-death (implied mean about 13 d). The authors state that nearly all of the delays rest on weakly-informed priors, often from other outbreaks, and that their posteriors largely track those priors. The onset-to-report delay is the exception, informed by the onset curve.

Case-fatality ratio: The prior is Beta(6.6, 13.4), with a mean that matches the CDC figure and the corrected central CFR in the 20 May report (McCabe and others, 2026). The authors say the CFR prior’s posterior largely tracks the prior.

Ascertainment and non-BVD background: Two surveillance systems, DRC passive community surveillance and Uganda point-of-entry/hospital surveillance, each capture a fraction of the true cases passing through them. The prior reflects the active case-finding of a declared Ebola response. The code centres the prior at logit(0.75). Reported suspected cases include an additive non-BVD background. The background is inferred to be the majority of the suspect pool. The DRC ascertainment, testing fraction and specimens analysed per suspect are each one value over the window, although ascertainment probably rose, so a change in any of them is read as a change in incidence.

Laboratory assumptions: Confirmation runs on the altona RealStar Filovirus Screen RT-PCR. The effective process sensitivity is about 98% with two controls, so the sensitivity prior is centred there. The severity-enrichment priors are not set from data.

Cross-border travel: The source population is fixed, and the traveller volume is given a Normal prior around the McCabe et al. figure. The export model counts every border crossing by an undetected infection as a possible detection in Uganda. A constant share of round trips is absorbed into the Uganda ascertainment, but a share that changes over the window is not.

Spatial structure and stream independence: The streams observe overlapping people but are fitted as conditionally independent given latent incidence, which can understate uncertainty. Ituri, Nord-Kivu and Haut-Uele are modelled individually, every other affected province is pooled into a fourth patch, and each is well mixed. The gravity kernel coupling the provinces is assumed, not measured, as there is no mobility or origin-destination data.

Aggregate data and model-based extrapolation: The authors do not have a line list, information on case definitions or reporting completeness, or access to the response’s internal data. Every estimate is therefore a model-based extrapolation under strong assumptions, not a measurement. The work is done outside the outbreak response, so changes in reporting practice are inferred from the reports rather than known. Almost every count is report-dated, so the epidemic’s timing is recovered mainly through the assumed delays.

Status of the analysis: The code and analysis were drafted by a language model and reviewed by people and by language models. The report is re-run as new data arrive, so the estimates change between updates, and it has not been peer reviewed.

Borrowed priors: Most quantities, including nearly all of the delays, the CFR and the laboratory assumptions, rest on weakly-informed priors, often from other outbreaks, and their posteriors largely track those priors. The onset-to-death delay and the genetic seeding bound do not propagate cross-outbreak or clock uncertainty.

Data revisions and discontinued streams: Later situation reports can revise earlier totals up or down as suspects are reclassified and newly-reporting health zones are added, and this revision process is not modelled. The suspected streams are no longer published, so the late window rests on the confirmed, laboratory, treatment-centre and onset data, and the suspected forecasts cannot be checked. The onset curve is digitised from a figure that each report redraws, so the counts carry scan error that the model treats as noise at a fixed scale.

Stream independence: The streams are fitted as conditionally independent given latent incidence, which can understate uncertainty.

Spatial and bed-model simplifications: The treatment-centre model carries one national bed capacity and demand, so it cannot represent local saturation. Ituri holds most of the occupied beds, so the national bed shortfall understates local unmet need. Spread inside a province is not represented. The province tables start on 15 June, and before then the provinces are informed only through the national streams. The zone stage is melded one way onto the joint fit, so the zone data do not update or correct the national and province estimates.

Sampling diagnostics: The joint fit passes the convergence checks with warnings. Its worst R-hat is 1.04 and its lowest bulk effective sample size is 43. Across all 12 fits the worst R-hat is 1.19, and the lowest bulk effective sample size is 13, both in the deaths (DRC) fit.

Primary outbreak data:

DRC situation reports: the DRC data come from the situation reports of the Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP, 2026).

Confirmed totals: 8978 confirmed cases and 4336 confirmed deaths at 2026-10-10.

Suspected totals, frozen after reclassification: 246 suspected deaths and 1077 suspected cases at 2026-05-26.

Daily new-suspect counts: read from 4 June.

Laboratory data: 755 specimens analysed at 2026-05-28.

Digitised onset curve: from SitRep 059 (12 July) onward, a raster figure of confirmed cases by symptom-onset date, digitised directly from the figure. The last total is 7132 at 2026-10-10.

Treatment-centre data: a patient-movement table (Tableau 6) from 13 June. At 2026-08-02 it shows 147 admissions, 22 in-care deaths, 93 rule-outs and 2 absconded.

Provincial and zone tables: Tableau 2 of the same situation reports.

Uganda exports: the cases and the one death exported across the border, from WHO situation reports and Disease Outbreak News. Three exported cases were dated 2026-05-23 and one export death 2026-05-14.

Auxiliary data:

Travel and population: cross-border traveller volume and source population from McCabe and others (2026). The traveller prior mean is 1871 (SD 200), and the source population is 4392200.

Province and zone geography: 2019 province populations from the DRC’s Institut National de la Statistique. Distances use WorldPop-weighted population centres.

Genetic data: a BEAST time tree of the first ten sequenced genomes places the TMRCA at a mean of 25 March 2026. A BEAST X reanalysis of 139 BDBV genomes reports an exponential-growth doubling time of 11.7 d (95% HPD 6.8-17.5).

Generation interval: Ebola virus disease serial interval (fitted Gamma, mean 15.3 d, SD 9.3 d, from 92 transmission pairs; WHO Ebola Response Team 2014).

Incubation period: from the 2007 Uganda outbreak (mean 6.3 d, 95% CI 5.2-7.3; MacNeil et al., 2010).

Onset-to-admission and onset-to-death delays: a Bayesian reanalysis (Funk and Abbott, 2026) of the 2012 Isiro Bundibugyo virus outbreak line list (Rosello and others, 2015).

Case-fatality prior: the CDC summary for the two previous BVD outbreaks.

Verheyden and Mudogo (13 Sep 2026)Observed Fatality or Observed Death? Differential Death Ascertainment and Provincial Mortality Heterogeneity during the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis does not attempt to estimate the true size of the 2026 BVD outbreak or a detection multiplier for total infections. Instead, it investigates why North Kivu reported a substantially higher cumulative case-fatality ratio (CFR) than Ituri Province, using a longitudinal reconstruction of DRC national situation reports (SitReps) through 13 September 2026. The central finding is that 415/1,507 (27.5%) classified positives in Ituri and 265/568 (46.7%) in North Kivu were already deceased when reported positive (Mantel-Haenszel OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.76-2.70), indicating that differential ascertainment (detection of cases alive versus after death) is a major driver of the provincial CFR gap rather than necessarily reflecting a true outbreak-size discrepancy.

The analysis does not produce an estimate of true outbreak size or a detection multiplier relative to confirmed cases. It reports only reported/confirmed case and death counts and CFR-related quantities. For context, confirmed cumulative counts at the freeze were by 13 September, the formal freeze, Ituri reported 5,659 cases and 2,583 deaths (45.6%) and North Kivu 1,281 cases and 797 deaths (62.2%), a 16.6-point gap. The key quantitative outputs are the dead-at-detection proportions (27.5% Ituri vs 46.7% North Kivu, Mantel-Haenszel OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.76–2.70) and the counterfactual compatibility calculation showing that applying a common 25% fatality rate among live-detected cases to the late-regime dead-at-detection shares would generate expected reported CFRs of 45.7% and 61.5%, respectively, close to the observed 13 September CFRs. No estimate of true infection numbers or under-ascertainment multiplier for total case burden is given.

Longitudinal ecological surveillance reconstruction: The authors designed a longitudinal ecological surveillance analysis using official DRC Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP) situation reports from the 17th Ebola epidemic, organized at province-by-SitRep level, to compare the proportion of newly confirmed cases already dead when detected (“dead-at-detection share”) between Ituri and North Kivu provinces.

Matched-SitRep comparison with Mantel-Haenszel and Bayesian binomial logistic modeling: The core analysis restricted comparisons to SitReps in which both Ituri and North Kivu contain definitionally compatible living/deceased splits, then used a Mantel-Haenszel comparison stratified by SitRep alongside a Bayesian binomial logistic model...fitted as a complementary analysis with province, reporting regime, and their interaction, applied to the same two-province dataset of 28 matched SitReps.

Counterfactual standardization (compatibility calculation): This method used a simple accounting identity, If π is the proportion of confirmed cases already deceased when detected and q is the eventual fatality among cases detected alive, then under a two-pathway completed-outcome accounting model the expected reported CFR is R = π + q(1-π), applied to the same Ituri/North Kivu provincial data to test whether ascertainment differences alone could reproduce the observed CFR gap, varying q from 0.10 to 0.50.

Postmortem-surveillance and death-location triangulation: Using operational indicators such as bodies swabbed relative to death alerts and death-location classification (community, health facility, CTE/CT), the analysis triangulated independent evidence of differential postmortem detection between the two provinces, e.g. in the three matched SitReps for which a comparable death-alert denominator and number of bodies swabbed could be reconstructed (72, 80 and 82), Ituri reported 163 bodies swabbed for 247 death alerts (66.0%), whereas North Kivu reported 118 for 120 (98.3%).

None of these methods estimate a true outbreak size or a detection multiplier for total infections; the analysis is explicit that it does not attempt latent incidence estimation: We did not fit a more elaborate latent epidemic simulation because the aggregate SitRep streams do not independently identify true incidence, outcome-specific detection probabilities, and biological fatality.

Two-pathway accounting structure: The counterfactual calculation assumes cases enter the confirmed series via only two pathways — detected alive or detected after death — formalized as If π is the proportion of confirmed cases already deceased when detected and q is the eventual fatality among cases detected alive, then under a two-pathway completed-outcome accounting model the expected reported CFR is R = π + q(1-π). The authors are explicit this is a compatibility analysis, not an estimator of infection-fatality risk.

Common eventual fatality (q) across provinces: The compatibility calculation assumes a shared eventual fatality probability among live-detected cases, tested across q values from 0.10 to 0.50, with an illustrative common value of 25% used to reproduce observed CFRs. This is explicitly a sensitivity sweep rather than a fixed single value.

Non-identifiability of latent incidence and fatality: The analysis structurally assumes it cannot and should not attempt to decompose true incidence, biological fatality, and ascertainment from aggregate counts alone, stating with aggregate SitRep counts alone, true incidence, biological fatality, live-case detection, and postmortem detection are not separately identifiable without strong external constraints, and treating this as a deliberate stop rule: when materially different combinations of latent incidence, fatality, and ascertainment can generate the same observed streams, the data do not support a unique decomposition.

Stratification by reporting regime rather than a constant province effect: Because the report-specific odds were heterogeneous, we did not interpret one common odds ratio as a time-invariant biological effect, the analysis assumes the ascertainment contrast varies by reporting regime (COUSP period SitReps 66-77 vs Task Force period 96-122) rather than being constant over time, and models this with a Bayesian province-by-regime interaction using weakly informative priors Weakly informative Normal(0, 2.5) priors were used for contrast coefficients and a wider Normal(0, 5) prior for the intercept.

Missingness treated as non-random and non-imputed: The analysis assumes missing fields should not be filled in, stating Missingness was treated as a feature of the surveillance record. We did not impute zero for absent fields and did not interpolate the primary living/deceased split across reports.

Aggregate, unlinked data: The authors state that the SitReps are aggregate operational reports rather than linked patient-level datasets, so a death classified in the laboratory section cannot be linked to an alert, admission, treatment history, symptom-onset date, or individual outcome trajectory.

Changing definitions and reconciliation: The authors note reporting definitions changed over time, some reports contain reconciliation corrections, and several operational fields are absent or incomplete. Relatedly, the primary split is available only on selected reports and may itself reflect which samples reached the laboratory.

Non-identifiability of biological fatality: The authors emphasize that neither the matched analysis nor the counterfactual standardization identifies the true infection-fatality risk. A latent decomposition would require patient-linked data or strong external constraints; without them, multiple combinations of incidence, mortality, and ascertainment remain observationally compatible.

Operational indicators not patient-linked: Postmortem swabbing and death-alert counts used for triangulation are described as limited: these are aggregate operational completion indicators; alert and swab counts are not patient-linked and can include carry-over.

Cannot rule out genuine clinical/capacity differences: The authors acknowledge the source-audited and model-based analyses support an ascertainment mechanism but also leave a credible pathway through which delayed presentation and constrained care could contribute to genuine mortality differences.

Health-zone analysis limited: Health-zone data confirm that neither province is internally homogeneous, but the current SitRep series does not provide the primary living/deceased laboratory split consistently at health-zone level.

Cannot quantify effect of parallel administrative structure: Regarding the AFC/M23-administered response in parts of North Kivu, the authors state we cannot quantify this pathway from the available aggregate SitReps, and offer it as one plausible, non-mutually-exclusive mechanism rather than an identified cause.

Primary outbreak data: the analysis relies on official DRC Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP) situation reports from the 17th Ebola epidemic, with twenty-eight SitReps provid[ing] a matched provincial living/deceased laboratory split forming the primary inferential series (SitReps 66, 67, 69, 70, 72, 73, 74, 77, 96, 97, 99, 101, 102, 104, 105, 108, 109, 110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119 and 122, per the document). Across these, the laboratory stream classified 1,507 new/report-period positives in Ituri, of whom 415 were deceased (27.5%), and 568 in North Kivu, of whom 265 were deceased (46.7%). Additional primary streams include provincial cumulative confirmed case/death counts, death-location classifications (community/health facility/CTE), postmortem swabbing and death-alert cascades, and hospital bed-occupancy data, all drawn from the same SitRep sequence.

Auxiliary data: the analysis references prior literature on ascertainment bias in outbreak fatality estimates and historical operational context, e.g. postmortem Ebola testing was operationalized in eastern DRC during and after the 2018-2020 epidemic, while community-based surveillance systems expanded the production and investigation of alerts and improved access to testing, and notes on a contemporary patient-level analysis from the same outbreak Contemporary patient-level reporting from the same outbreak has already cautioned that early observed deaths cannot be interpreted as a CFR when final outcomes and denominators are incomplete. No travel, demographic, or cross-border datasets are used, as the analysis is confined to within-DRC provincial surveillance comparison.

hierarchy.lvl3: Epistorm (27 Jul 2026)Ebola Bundibugyo Virus — DRC · Spread Risk Assessment #7 · Local Transmission Scenarios
Epistorm (27 Jul 2026)Ebola Bundibugyo Virus — DRC · Spread Risk Assessment #7 · Local Transmission Scenarios

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis uses a stochastic, metapopulation transmission model (built on the GLEAM framework) to project the trajectory of the DRC Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak under different isolation-intervention scenarios, rather than to produce a single “true size” nowcast. The report presents a stochastic, metapopulation transmission model built using the GLEAM framework, incorporating transmission occurring in the hospital, community, and through funerals, and explicitly modeling isolation protocols through ETC. The model is calibrated against confirmed Ituri case counts allowing for under-ascertainment, yielding posterior R₀ ≈ 2.02 (90% CrI [1.72, 2.47]) and empirical doubling time 12.9 d (90% CrI [10.7, 15.6]), and forward projections across three isolation scenarios (30%, 50%, 75%) show widely diverging outcomes by 30 September 2026, ranging from near-control under high isolation to outbreak sizes exceeding 20,000 cases in three-quarters of trajectories under low isolation.

The calibration itself implies a range for true cumulative symptomatic cases in Ituri as of 18 July 2026: the simulated cumulative symptomatic onsets in Ituri by 18 July are required to lie in the window [2,090, 5,225], allowing ascertainment as low as 40%, against a confirmed count of 2,090 at that date.

For forward projection to 1 August 2026 (DRC-wide), the headline figures are: Cumulative symptomatic cases: iso30 5,551 [3,352 - 8,245], iso50 4,991 [2,981 - 7,318], iso75 4,414 [2,645 - 6,363], with active cases (I + H + ETC): iso30 1,287 [651 - 2,342], iso50 870 [423 - 1,630], iso75 462 [206 - 946] and new symptomatic cases per day: iso30 158 [75 - 298], iso50 95 [44 - 195], iso75 42 [16 - 96].

For 30 September 2026, outcomes are reported as probabilities rather than point estimates: probability of ≥20,000 cumulative symptomatic cases is <1% under 75% isolation, 20% under 50%, and 75% under 30%; and the probability of exceeding 10,000 cases by 30 September is 98% under 30% isolation, 69% under 50% and 9% under 75%, while for the higher threshold of ≥20,000 cases the corresponding probabilities are 75%, 20% and <1%.

GLEAM metapopulation model with care-pathway SEIHFR dynamics: This is a stochastic, spatially explicit simulation model in which GLEAM (Global Epidemic and Mobility Model) is an Africa-wide metapopulation network coupled by daily commuting matrices and origin-destination passenger flows, with within-basin compartmental dynamics simulated as a discrete-time multinomial chain-binomial process. The compartmental structure follows a Legrand-like SEIHFR scheme, extended to incorporate three potential outcomes an infectious individual could experience — community, HCF-only, and isolation-to-ETC branches — and it applies to DRC (17 basins plus Goma) and Uganda.

Two-stage Approximate Bayesian Computation calibration: The model’s epidemiological parameters are fitted to outbreak data using ABC rather than a direct estimator. Stage 1 conditions on observed cross-border importations from Ituri to Uganda, requiring exactly one Uganda importation by 14 May 2026 and exactly one further importation in the window 14 to 18 May 2026. Stage 2 conditions the Stage-1 posterior on the cumulative laboratory-confirmed count in Ituri at 18 July 2026 (2,090 cases) allowing ascertainment as low as 40%, requiring the simulated cumulative symptomatic onsets in Ituri by 18 July to lie in the window [2,090, 5,225]. This calibration applies to the Ituri source population within DRC, with sensitivity noted in that posterior medians of R₀ and Td are stable when the ascertainment floor is relaxed or tightened, though a formal sensitivity table at alternative floors is deferred to a subsequent update.

Scenario-based forward projection: Using the calibrated posterior, the model projects DRC-wide outcomes under three isolation targets. Forward projections evaluate three target isolation rates, 30%, 50% and 75%, each phased in at 2 percentage points per day from 20 May 2026 across DRC (17 basins plus the Goma catchment) until the scenario target is reached, while Uganda is held at a constant 80% isolation from the start of the intervention window. This produces cumulative case, active case, daily incidence, and Rt trajectories, plus probabilities of exceeding case thresholds, all aggregated to DRC.

Calibration priors: The model draws R₀ from U(1.2, 5.0), incubation period TE from U(5, 10) days (Erlang-2, two-stage latent), and outbreak start date from U(15 Feb, 15 Mar 2026), with these priors filtered through the two-stage ABC against importation and case-count evidence.

Ascertainment floor: The baseline analysis allows ascertainment as low as 40% (window [2,090, 5,225]) when calibrating to the 18 July Ituri confirmed count; this single assumption directly sets the implied detection gap used to anchor the model.

Care-pathway dwell times and case-fatality ratios: The model fixes compartment-specific parameters including community dwell time 9.6 d, onset-to-HCF 5 d (routine) vs 2 d (isolation track), HCF-to-ETC transit 3 d, HCF stay 4.6 d, funeral period 2 d, HCF admission probability 0.80, CFR of 0.50 (non-hospitalised), 0.45 (regular HCF), 0.30 (ETC), an R₀ split of 0.44:0.22:0.34 across community/HCF/funeral transmission, and a residual HCF-isolation transmission factor of 0.1, several sourced from literature/prior outbreaks.

Isolation ramp and intervention structure: Isolation is phased in at 2 percentage points per day from 20 May 2026 across DRC (17 basins plus Goma) until reaching target (30%, 50%, or 75%), with Uganda held at a constant 80% isolation, and this ramp and case-finding timing are applied homogeneously across all symptomatic cases, though real-world coverage varies by location and over time.

Mobility and seeding: No mobility reductions between subpopulations are assumed — no behavioral reduction, no border closure, and no seasonality in transmissibility is modeled, and the epidemic is seeded with 5 infectious cases in Ituri on the inferred start date, with every other basin fully susceptible and reached only through mobility.

Calibration data is limited to a single date and sparse importation counts: Stage 1 uses only evidence of importations from Ituri → Uganda (exact-count, no tolerance band), without directly fitting within-Ituri incidence, while Stage 2 adds only a single cumulative count at one date. Alternative acceptance rules or additional within-basin time-points would shift the posteriors.

Projections beyond the calibration date are model-driven: Calibration extends only to the 18 July 2026 confirmed-case evidence, and projections beyond that date are model-driven and depend on assumptions about isolation timing and intensity.

Borrowed timing parameters may not match 2026 operations: Isolation-track timings (Tiso = 2 d, HCF → ETC ≈ 3 d) follow the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response, which may not exactly match the 2026 operational reality. The residual nosocomial channel in the iso branch (0.1·βH) is a modelling assumption, sensitivity-testable.

Static mobility and homogeneous intervention coverage: Mobility is held static across the simulation, with no behavioral reduction, no border closure modeled, and no seasonality in transmissibility; informal cross-border movement may be under-captured. The isolation ramp and case-finding timings are applied homogeneously across all symptomatic cases, while real-world coverage varies by location and over time.

Scope exclusion: International dissemination is out of scope for this report (see Reports #3 and #4).

Primary outbreak data: DRC cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases (3,360) and confirmed deaths (1,487) as of 27 July 2026 across 48 health zones in five provinces, with 733 patients currently hospitalised in isolation; Uganda confirmed cases (20, including 2 deaths); the Ituri confirmed case count used for calibration, 2,090 cases as of 18 July 2026; and cross-border importation event counts used in Stage 1 calibration, requiring exactly one Uganda importation by 14 May 2026 and exactly one further importation in the window 14 to 18 May 2026.

Auxiliary data: IATA / OAG passenger origin-destination data and daily commuting matrices for mobility coupling; natural-history parameters from the 2007-2008 Uganda BVD outbreak data (Wamala et al.); and case-finding timing parameters following the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response.

hierarchy.lvl3: Verheyden and Mudogo (27 Jul 2026)Sixteen Days Undetected: Growth Dynamics and the Case for Pre-Positioned Response Capacity in the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease
Verheyden and Mudogo (27 Jul 2026)Sixteen Days Undetected: Growth Dynamics and the Case for Pre-Positioned Response Capacity in the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease

records.content:
Outbreak, Democratic Republic of the Congo

Read the analysis

This analysis aims to characterize, rather than estimate a single “true size” figure for, the 2026 BDBV outbreak: specifically its early growth rate, the date transmission actually began (back-calculated), and whether the rising case-fatality ratio reflects worsening severity or a detection artefact. The authors analysed a corrected daily surveillance series (65 observations, 14 May-27 July 2026) using non-linear least-squares regression and a Bayesian Poisson growth model fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo, with five sensitivity analyses. The headline findings are that early confirmed cases grew at 0·1261 per day (95% CI 0·0885-0·1636), a doubling time of 5·50 days (4·24-7·83), three-fold faster than previous BDBV outbreaks (15-18 days); Bayesian back-calculation placed transmission onset on 19 April 2026 (95% highest-density interval 9-27 April), 16 days before the WHO alert and 25 days before laboratory confirmation; and confirmed case-fatality ratio rose from 12·1% to 44·3%, with a cross-classification analysis supporting progressive reclassification rather than increasing virulence. A later full-series logistic model produces a provisional outbreak-size (final-size, K) projection, but the authors flag this estimate as unstable across successive data extensions.

This analysis does not produce a single “true outbreak size” figure comparable to under-ascertainment models; its primary quantitative outputs are growth rate, doubling time, and back-calculated onset date. Two quantities come closest to a case-burden estimate. First, back-calculated circulating-case numbers at key pre-declaration dates: at a doubling time of 5·5 days, this detection lag alone corresponds to approximately six-fold case growth before international response mechanisms activated: at the WHO alert date, the model implies 4-13 circulating cases (median 8); by declaration on 15 May, 20-38 cases (median 28). Second, a provisional final-size (K) projection from the full-series logistic model: over the full 65-observation series (14 May-27 July), growth rate fell to r = 0·0364 per day (Tᵈ = 19·02 days), and a logistic model was preferred by AIC (K ≈ 6,166), confirming substantial deceleration as response capacity scaled - though the authors treat this plateau estimate as provisional: successive one-week extensions of this series have shifted the fitted asymptote from K ≈ 2,333 to K ≈ 3,002 to K ≈ 6,166 (29% then 105% change). The most recent logistic K estimate carries a 95% CI of 4413-7920. The authors explicitly caution that this figure has more than doubled across two successive one-week extensions of the data window and is reported here for model-comparison completeness, not as a dependable final-size projection.

Classical growth-rate regression: Cumulative case counts C(t) were modelled as C(t) = C₀·exp(r·t), where r is the exponential growth rate and doubling time Tᵈ = ln(2)/r; the early-phase model (14-27 May, pre-discontinuity) was fitted by non-linear least squares to 12 daily observations, and a logistic model was fitted to the full 65-observation series and compared against the exponential model by Akaike Information Criterion. This method is applied to DRC-national confirmed daily case counts.

Bayesian hierarchical growth/back-calculation model: A Bayesian hierarchical model (Poisson likelihood, weakly informative Normal priors, fitted by Markov Chain Monte Carlo in PyMC3) estimated growth rate r, initial case count C₀, and t_back - the number of days before the first situation report that transmission began - with full posterior uncertainty propagation. (The verified implementation used a Normal rather than Poisson likelihood with an estimated observation-noise scale.) It is applied to the same DRC-national pre-discontinuity daily series, with five pre-specified sensitivity analyses varying priors, the fitting window, and the observation-model distribution.

CFR trajectory and cross-classification analysis: CFR was calculated at each reporting date; at the earliest date with disaggregated confirmed and suspected case and death data (21 May 2026), confirmed and suspected CFR were compared by two-sample z-test, and the temporal CFR trajectory was examined for consistency with progressive reclassification of suspected deaths into the confirmed category versus an irregular pattern consistent with genuine severity change. This uses DRC-national aggregate surveillance data, supplemented by a single cross-classification snapshot from external sources.

Growth-model functional form: Cumulative case counts were modelled as C(t) = C₀·exp(r·t) for the early phase, with a logistic alternative, C(t) = K / [1 + ((K − C₀)/C₀)·exp(−r·t)], fitted to the full series. The choice between exponential and logistic forms drives the instability in the final-size (K) estimate.

Bayesian priors: Weakly informative priors were used: r ∼ Normal(0.13, 0.05), C₀ ∼ Normal(33, 10), σ ∼ HalfNormal(20). Sensitivity analyses varied these: an optimistic prior (r ∼ Normal(0.11, 0.02)) gave posterior median r = 0.124 and implied onset 17 April, while a pessimistic prior (r ∼ Normal(0.15, 0.03)) gave posterior median r = 0.137 and implied onset 20 April, with back-calculated onset across these variants ranging 17-22 April consistent with the primary estimate (19 April, 95% HDI 9-27 April).

Single index case: The back-calculated parameter t_back gives the outbreak start date assuming a single index case (C = 1) at the back-calculated start. Back-calculation assumes a single index case; multiple early spillover events (as suggested for the 2012 BDBV outbreak) would shift the estimated start date later, making 19 April a conservative (earlier) estimate under the single-introduction assumption.

Mongbwalu cluster excluded from formal estimation: The authors do not incorporate reported evidence of a possible earlier, undetected February 2026 death cluster into the formal back-calculation, which would launder soft, uncertain evidence into false statistical precision, and instead report it as an explicit plausibility bound: if this cluster reflects genuine early BDBV transmission, true onset could lie anywhere between early February 2026 and the estimate of 19 April 2026.

Historical comparison data are approximate: Historical BDBV doubling-time comparisons are approximate; formal statistical comparison requires digitised onset curves from 2007 and 2012 primary sources, which are ongoing.

Single index case assumption: Back-calculation assumes a single index case; multiple early spillover events would shift the estimated start date later, making 19 April a conservative (earlier) estimate under the single-introduction assumption.

CFR interpretation based on limited data: CFR interpretation rests on aggregate surveillance data and a single cross-classification snapshot; line-list data stratified by onset date, confirmation date, care setting, and outcome would enable formal survival analysis.

Mechanistic explanations are inferential: The mechanistic discussion of growth-rate drivers is inferential; testing any individual mechanism requires appropriately controlled epidemiological studies.

Final-size projection is unstable: The epidemic curve does not yet contain enough information to fix a final size with confidence - a caveat substantiated directly where extending the data window by a further week nearly doubled the logistic model’s estimated final size.

Data completeness and corrections: The daily series is not entirely complete: ten dates lack confirmed-case counts in the primary source and were excluded rather than interpolated - a larger set than an earlier draft of this manuscript reported (five dates), which is flagged for the authors to reconcile rather than silently revised. Earlier weekly-aggregated extractions were superseded: the original analysis relied on weekly aggregated case counts (n = 3 for the early-phase model); this has been resolved using the complete corrected daily surveillance series.

Uncorroborated earlier cluster: A co-investigator raised the possibility of an earlier, undetected cluster in Mongbwalu health zone during review; this evidence is reported transparently but has not been incorporated into the back-calculation analysis, as doing so would require independent verification that lies beyond the scope of the present dataset.

Primary outbreak data: cumulative confirmed case counts and deaths were extracted from a corrected daily surveillance series (65 observations, 14 May-27 July 2026) drawn from the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository of digitised DRC INSP situation reports. This corrected series superseded an earlier extraction from WHO AFRO Weekly External Situation Reports, which was found on reanalysis to contain date-alignment and transcription errors. Checkpoints were cross-validated against independently published figures (15 July: 2,124 cases/828 deaths, WHO Disease Outbreak News; 18 July: 2,344/930, NICD; 27 July: 3,360/1,487, ECDC). Ten reporting dates lack confirmed-case counts in the source and were excluded rather than interpolated. Epidemiological context and the 21 May 2026 cross-classification data (confirmed vs suspected cases/deaths) were taken from Mwamba et al. and Tonen-Wolyec and Bélec.

Auxiliary data: historical BDBV outbreak parameters, including the index Uganda epidemic (2007-2008; 116-149 cases; CFR 25-34%) and the subsequent Isiro, DRC epidemic (2012; 52-62 cases; CFR 49-54%), used as a comparator for doubling-time and CFR. Community versus facility CFR figures from the 2012 DRC outbreak (93·8% community CFR vs 22·2% among survivors identified by retrospective serology) are used to corroborate the ascertainment-lag mechanism, and historical care-setting CFRs from 2007 Uganda and 2012 DRC are reported as a reference baseline.

hierarchy.lvl3: Verheyden, Mudogo and Jacquet (20 Jul 2026)How Predictable Was the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak? A Rolling-Origin Evaluation of Short-Term Forecast Models, an Empirically Recalibrated Bayesian Model, and a Data-Driven Baseline–Bayesian Ensemble, Using Daily Surveillance Data

Verheyden, Mudogo and Jacquet (20 Jul 2026)How Predictable Was the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak? A Rolling-Origin Evaluation of Short-Term Forecast Models, an Empirically Recalibrated Bayesian Model, and a Data-Driven Baseline–Bayesian Ensemble, Using Daily Surveillance Data

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis is a retrospective forecasting evaluation, not an under-detection or “true size” estimation study: it tests how accurately simple and more complex statistical models could have forecast the already-confirmed case and death trajectory of the 2026 BVD outbreak using only data available in real time. The authors refitted two prespecified operational models using only data available at that time: a recent seven-increment baseline and a Bayesian negative-binomial surveillance-maturity model fitted by full Markov Chain Monte Carlo on complete available history, alongside a Gompertz growth model...fitted identically at every origin as a phenomenological benchmark. The main finding is that Routine SitRep data supported useful short-term forecasting, but no single model was best on every criterion, and a data-driven combination of two complementary, individually weaker-in-some-respect models measurably outperformed either alone for one of two outcomes evaluated; this paper does not independently estimate a “true” outbreak size distinct from confirmed counts.

This analysis does not produce an independent “true outbreak size” estimate distinct from confirmed/reported counts; it forecasts future values of the confirmed case and death series itself. The headline forward-looking output is from the most recent origin: Forecasts from the most recent eligible origin (20 July 2026; 2,473 cumulative confirmed cases, 999 cumulative confirmed deaths) are reported for all three horizons as a genuinely forward-looking scenario, not yet scoreable against observation. Within that output, the authors flag one figure as an upper-scenario extrapolation: The 21-day Bayesian death forecast (median 2,286.8, more than double the 999 deaths recorded at the origin) is reported without adjustment because it is a faithful output of the validated, checkpoint-verified pipeline, but is flagged here as an aggressive extrapolation that should be read as an upper scenario rather than a precise point estimate, noting that the ensemble (not tabulated here; see Table 2 for validated weights) provides a more conservative central figure by construction for this reason. Across all models and 55 rolling-origin evaluations, performance (not a single outbreak-size estimate) is summarized by median absolute percentage error and interval coverage at 7-, 14-, and 21-day horizons, e.g. the baseline retained the lowest or near-lowest median point error at every horizon (median absolute percentage error 3·2%, 5·9%, and 10·7% at 7, 14, and 21 days) for cases, and the recalibrated Bayesian model improved death forecasts on both accuracy and calibration at every horizon (7-day median absolute percentage error 10·3%→7·7%...14-day...22·5%→11·4%...21-day...33·6%→23·5%).

Baseline recent-trend model: This is a simple operational forecasting rule applied to the national confirmed-case and death series. The baseline model assumed that the recent mean reporting pace would continue over the forecast horizon. For valid one-calendar-day increments...the expected daily increment at origin T was the mean of the seven most recent valid increments. Predictive intervals came from bootstrap resampling of the recent valid increments (20,000 replicates), with resampled negative increments truncated at zero, producing a point forecast and interval for confirmed cases/deaths at national level.

Bayesian negative-binomial surveillance-maturity model: This is a probabilistic count model fitted to the complete national daily incidence history at each forecast origin, explicitly representing a detected change in surveillance capacity. For valid daily incident counts over the complete available history at each forecast origin...S is an indicator equal to 1 on and after 28 May 2026 and 0 before it; the level shift attributable to the surveillance-maturity discontinuity; separate trend slopes for the post- and pre-discontinuity regimes; serial dependence on the previous observed and expected count (an INGARCH-type structure); and the negative-binomial dispersion parameter. The raw model’s forecasts were further corrected by a prospective, quality-gated empirical recalibration using only errors already realised at earlier, forecast-maturity-qualified origins, applied to national confirmed case and death counts.

Gompertz growth curve (phenomenological benchmark): Cumulative cases or deaths were modelled using the Gompertz function C(t) = K·exp{−a·exp(−bt)}, refitted at each origin by non-linear least squares subject to positivity constraints, with predictive uncertainty from parametric bootstrap. This model was tested at national level but is not carried forward as a recommended forecasting tool: its 80% predictive-interval coverage was the poorest of all candidates at every horizon and outcome evaluated.

Data-driven ensemble: This method pools simulated trajectories from the baseline and recalibrated Bayesian model rather than averaging published intervals. At each origin and horizon, a proportion w of a combined predictive sample was drawn from the baseline’s bootstrap trajectories and the remaining (1−w) from the Bayesian model’s recalibrated posterior predictive trajectories...The mixing weight w was selected separately for each outcome and horizon using a strictly prospective, expanding-origin procedure. This is applied to the same national confirmed case/death series as the component models.

Surveillance-maturity discontinuity: The Bayesian model structurally assumes a single step-change in ascertainment rather than a continuous trend, located at a specific date. A changepoint scan (PELT and binary segmentation, cross-checked with a robust outlier statistic) identified a discontinuity in daily case increments on 28 May 2026 (robust z-score 13·0 against the trailing week), two days after a documented Africa CDC surveillance-decentralisation plan, providing external corroboration that this reflects a change in case-ascertainment capacity rather than transmission alone. The model represents this with weakly informative priors...(ω0 ∼ Normal(log of the median positive recent increment, 2); ω1’ ∼ Normal(0, 0.2); ω2 ∼ Normal(0, 2) under the prospective, no-lookahead scenario reported as primary; Φ ∼ Half-Normal(20)).

Baseline continuation assumption: The simple baseline model assumes recent reporting pace is the best predictor of near-term future pace, with the recent mean reporting pace...continue[d] over the forecast horizon...the mean of the seven most recent valid increments, an assumption that breaks down explicitly at a few early origins where fewer than seven valid increments existed due to reporting gaps.

Gompertz asymptote identifiability: The excluded Gompertz model assumes the epidemic has a definable saturating asymptote; a fit was flagged unstable if the estimated asymptote exceeded 20 times the cumulative total at the forecast origin, and this assumption was found not to hold given the outbreak’s growth stage, per the Methods and Discussion.

Recalibration and ensemble validation: The recalibration correction and ensemble weights are selected using a prospective, no-lookahead procedure (median forecast error over earlier mature origins) but are both derived and tested on the same 55 origins, rather than on a fully independent dataset, as discussed under Limitations.

Health-zone heterogeneity not modelled: all evaluated models used only the national aggregate series; health-zone-level heterogeneity, which the underlying surveillance data show to be substantial, was not modelled explicitly and is a natural extension.

Recalibration and ensemble procedures validated only in-sample: the empirical recalibration and ensemble weighting procedures, though strictly prospective within this dataset, were both selected and validated using the same 55 origins reported in Table 2; genuine held-out validation on a separate outbreak, as performed for the forecast-maturity relationship itself, was not attempted for these two specific procedures and would strengthen confidence in their generalisability.

Illustrative loss-function parameters: the asymmetric operational loss function’s cost parameters (λ, γ) were chosen for illustration rather than derived from a documented capacity-planning cost structure; operational adopters should re-derive these from their own context.

Forecast maturity constrains but does not eliminate extrapolation risk: a forecast-maturity ratio at or above 1 constrains but does not eliminate the risk of aggressive long-horizon extrapolation from a still-evolving outbreak, and this risk should continue to be monitored and reported explicitly rather than assumed away by the maturity criterion alone.

Data gaps and discrepancies: Seven calendar dates lack a national confirmed-case observation...and are retained as explicitly missing rather than imputed or interpolated, and a one-case discrepancy was identified and corrected during cross-checking, which the authors note is smaller than the between-run resampling noise already documented for this pipeline (±10 units) and did not warrant refitting.

Primary outbreak data: Daily cumulative confirmed cases and deaths were extracted from national situation reports published by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) and cross-validated against independent contemporaneous sources (WHO Disease Outbreak News, Africa CDC situation updates, NICD, and ECDC epidemiological updates) where available, spanning 14 May to 20 July 2026 (68 calendar dates; 61 dates with a numeric national report), publicly archived at the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data GitHub repository...which we accessed and archived on 20 July 2026.

Auxiliary data: for external validation of the forecast-maturity finding, the authors used a completed historical outbreak dataset: an independent completed 77-week outbreak (North Kivu/Ituri, 2018-2020) using a deliberately simpler method.

hierarchy.lvl3: Kim, Mills and Donnelly (21 Jun 2026)Cross-border travel patterns affect magnitude estimates for the Ebola Bundibugyo epidemic
Kim, Mills and Donnelly (21 Jun 2026)Cross-border travel patterns affect magnitude estimates for the Ebola Bundibugyo epidemic

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis attempts to place an upper bound on the true number of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) early in the 2026 epidemic by working backward from cases exported to and confirmed in Uganda. The authors estimated an upper bound on the likely burden of Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo early in the unfolding 2026 epidemic based on the number of cases imported and confirmed in Uganda. The method is a modification of the standard “geographic spread” approach that explicitly accounts for short-duration cross-border trips and for the fact that all early imported cases had specifically travelled to seek healthcare, which substantially affected burden estimates, highlighting both the potential severity of the epidemic in its early phase and the critical need to consider local epidemiological contexts when applying geographic spread approaches. The paper reports two scenarios (three imported cases versus zero imported cases after excluding healthcare-seekers, each with and without accounting for travel duration), but the actual numeric results table was not included in the provided file, so only the qualitative pattern of results (wider intervals and higher central estimates when duration is accounted for) is available here.

The numeric results table (Table 1) referenced in the text was not included in the provided document, so specific central estimates and confidence intervals cannot be reported here. The text describes the pattern of results qualitatively: with three imported cases, accounting for the observed pattern of trip durations from Ituri and Nord Kivu, the DRC, to Uganda substantially increased the central estimates and widened the 95% confidence intervals compared to not accounting for travel durations within our framework and to those reported recently. In the zero-imported-cases scenario, the central estimates and the lower confidence limits were uninformative (zero by definition); however, the upper confidence limits provided informative likely upper bounds for the early BVD burden in the DRC, which can be used to inform epidemic responses. The only concrete numeric figure given is a methodological input, not a case estimate: the 95% Poisson-likelihood-based confidence interval for the rate of exported cases based on observing zero exported cases is (0, 1.92), which is then divided by the detection probability to yield the DRC case estimate (value not stated in the available text).

Geographic spread approach with travel-duration adjustment: This is a back-calculation method that estimates the true case burden in a source population from the number of cases detected after crossing into a neighboring country, generalized here to incorporate travel duration. A geographic spread approach is often used to estimate the true burden of infectious disease cases in a source population by leveraging statistical signals generated by cases exported and reported elsewhere. The authors state the method must carefully consider the specific epidemiological contexts that generate these signals; notably, when travel durations are short relative to the infection-to-detection interval, infected travellers may return home before detection, unlike prior applications of this approach that leveraged international air travel. The method is applied to the DRC source population (Ituri, and Ituri plus Nord Kivu as an alternative scope) using Uganda-confirmed imported cases as the detection signal, and the authors generalized the method further to obtain the overall probability of detection while travelling as a weighted average over different durations of travel and different infection-to-detection intervals, with sensitivity analyses varying travel-duration data source (March 2020 versus April 2019 border dashboards) and whether to use all three early imported cases or zero (after excluding healthcare-seeking travel).

Healthcare-seeking exclusion as a structural adjustment: As a distinct structural refinement rather than merely a parameter sensitivity, the authors re-ran the estimate excluding the imported cases that were specifically healthcare-seeking trips, since this healthcare-seeking behaviour violates the key assumption of the conventional geographic spread approach that individuals in the source population have an equal probability of travelling regardless of infection status. This produces the “zero imported cases” scenario noted above, applied to the same DRC (Ituri / Ituri and Nord Kivu) source population.

Travel duration categories and probabilities: The baseline scenario classifies trips into three durations — (a) less than 1 day (64.7%), (b) 1 day to 1 week (25.9%) and (c) longer than 1 week (9.4%) — from the March 2020 IOM dashboard, with an alternative scenario using (a) less than 1 day (47.4%), (b) 1 day to 1 week (45.4%) and (c) longer than 1 week (7.2%) from the April 2019 dashboard. Fixed median travel durations were assigned within categories: for the ‘less than 1 day’ and ‘1 day to 1 week’ travel duration categories, we assigned the fixed median travel durations of 0.5 and 4 days, respectively; for the ‘longer than 1 week’ category, we assumed an indefinite stay, indicating that infected travellers remained in Uganda long enough to be detected there.

Infection-to-detection interval: The delay from infection to detection uses the Gamma incubation distribution described above with median times of 10, 15 and 20 days, following McCabe et al., discretized at the day level, combined in a weighted average across durations to obtain an overall detection probability while travelling.

Equal-travel-probability assumption and its violation: The standard geographic spread approach assumes individuals in the source population have equal probability of travelling regardless of infection status; the authors note this healthcare-seeking behaviour violates the key assumption of the conventional geographic spread approach that individuals in the source population have an equal probability of travelling regardless of infection status, which is why they also run a zero-imported-case scenario excluding healthcare-seeking travellers.

No travel between detection and recovery: Individuals were assumed not to travel between detection and recovery.

Source population size: The estimate scales directly with the assumed source population, and the authors note our estimates are expected to change proportionally to the assumed source population size and could thus be biased if the assumed source population sizes did not accurately reflect the catchment population of those travelling to Uganda, [since] those residing near the DRC–Uganda border probably have a substantially different probability of travelling to Uganda compared with those living further away from the border.

Source population and catchment uncertainty: The authors note their estimates are expected to change proportionally to the assumed source population size and could thus be biased if the assumed source population sizes did not accurately reflect the catchment population of those travelling to Uganda, since those residing near the DRC–Uganda border probably have a substantially different probability of travelling to Uganda compared with those living further away from the border.

Differential infection risk among travellers: The authors acknowledge that individuals who can afford to travel to seek healthcare abroad may also have different baseline infection risks compared with the general population.

Knowledge gap on cross-border dynamics: This knowledge gap suggests that a better understanding of the complex cross-border crossing dynamics will help obtain more robust estimates of the true case burden using this geographic spread approach.

Missing trip-duration data for the relevant period: Trip-duration data were not available for the period when early imported cases were confirmed in Uganda, so the analysis relies on short-duration trip patterns being inferred from personal communication and historical dashboards rather than contemporaneous data.

Generalizability of the method: The authors note the approach’s reliability and generalizability depend on a careful consideration of these real-world contexts, distinguishing this epidemic from prior applications of the geographic spread method that assumed detection regardless of travel duration.

Primary outbreak data: Uganda-confirmed imported BVD cases, with until 21 June 2026, all 15 BVD cases imported and confirmed in Uganda being “Congolese nationals who came to Uganda to seek medical care,” and an earlier subset of the first three confirmed imported cases used in the main scenario comparisons.

Auxiliary data: travel-duration distributions from the March 2020 Uganda–DRC Border Flow Monitoring Dashboard by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), [showing] 90.6% of trips to Uganda from Ituri and Nord Kivu, the DRC, lasted a week or less, with 64.7% comprising day trips, and a comparator dataset where similar trends were observed in the April 2019 Uganda–DRC Border Flow Monitoring Dashboard data, with 92.8% of trips lasting a week or less. Daily traveller counts and source population sizes were borrowed from an earlier analysis: data on the daily number of travellers from Ituri (n = 1,871) and both Ituri and Nord Kivu (n = 4,339) to Uganda were obtained from McCabe et al., and the corresponding source population sizes were also obtained from McCabe et al.: Ituri (n = 4,392,200) and both Ituri and Nord Kivu (n = 13,392,200). The incubation/infection-to-detection delay distribution was also borrowed: the delay from infection to detection was modelled using a Gamma distribution for the incubation period (shape 2.52, rate 0.40), shifted by an assumed delay from symptom onset to clinical detection to give median times from infection to detection of 10, 15 and 20 days, following McCabe et al.

hierarchy.lvl3: Oraby, Falay and Ndeffo-Mbah (17 Jun 2026)Impact of Detection-Isolation-Leakage on the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebolavirus Outbreak
Oraby, Falay and Ndeffo-Mbah (17 Jun 2026)Impact of Detection-Isolation-Leakage on the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebolavirus Outbreak

records.content: Read the analysis

This analysis uses a Bayesian compartmental transmission model to estimate how much “isolation leakage” — patients leaving isolation facilities before full recovery — has amplified the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in Ituri Province, DRC, rather than directly estimating a single “true outbreak size” multiplier against confirmed cases. The authors expand the standard SEIHFR model to include an isolation-leakage compartment L and an undetected infectious compartment U, creating the new detection-isolation-leakage SEUIHLF3R model, fitted to surveillance data from Ituri Province during the 17th DRC Ebola epidemic using Bayesian methods. The central finding is that R0 = 3.67 (95% HDI: 2.0-5.7), with eliminating leakage reducing cumulative infections by about one-third, from 1,120 to 764, and that counterfactual scenarios of doubled or tripled leakage push cumulative actual infections substantially higher.

The headline model output is cumulative “actual (reported and unreported) infections” over the 14 May–17 June 2026 window in Ituri Province, estimated at posterior-median values under several leakage scenarios. At the fitted (baseline) leakage rate, cumulative actual (reported and unreported) infections is 1,120; removing leakage altogether with ρ = 0 lowers cumulative actual... infections from 1,120 at the fitted rate to 764, while doubling and tripling leakage increase cumulative infections to 1,478 and 1,800, respectively. Separately, the model’s reported-case output (the subset of actual infections that are detected) is most sensitive, climbing from 677 with no leakage to 1,575 at 3ρ̂, and reported deaths grow more moderately from 240 to 350 across the same range. These are posterior medians; every projected trajectory and derived summary computed across draws is reported using the posterior median and a 95% highest-density interval (HDI), though the specific HDI brackets for the 1,120/764/1,478/1,800 figures are presented in a table not fully reproduced in the extracted text. For context, actual surveillance reported 896 total confirmed cases... as of 17 June 2026, the same cutoff as the model’s end-of-window estimates, though the analysis does not itself state a ratio between its “actual infections” output and this confirmed count.

Bayesian compartmental SEUIHLF3R model: This is a mechanistic transmission model, an extension of the standard Ebola SEIHFR framework, that adds compartments for undetected community infections and for patients who leak out of isolation. It is fitted to surveillance data from Ituri Province during the 17th DRC Ebola epidemic using Bayesian methods, drawing on daily Ituri surveillance data, escapee counts, and isolation census records. The model produces posterior estimates of R0, the leakage rate, detection probability, and projected cumulative “actual infections” (reported plus unreported) via counterfactual simulation, applied at the Ituri provincial level as a single homogeneously-mixing population.

Forward counterfactual scenario simulation: Using the fitted posterior, the authors ran scenario analyses varying leakage rate, re-isolation rate, isolation speed, detection intensity, and safe-burial ascertainment to project cumulative actual infections, reported cases, and deaths under each scenario, again scoped to Ituri Province. Control measures were evaluated using forward counterfactual simulation based on the fitted posterior and without re-estimation.

Fixed natural-history and funeral-process parameters: The authors fix the natural-history and funeral-process parameters, T_U, c_U, γ_U, µ_U, ν, ν_H, and m_F, using externally specified community infectious duration T_U and community fatality probability c_U to reduce structural non-identifiability in the undetected and funeral-transmission pathways, justified because the reported case and death time series cannot separately identify the undetected burden, the community fatality probability, the death-detection probability, and the funeral infectiousness.
